title: Seroprevalence of Canine Leishmaniasis and the Public Health Risk of Asymptomatic Dogs in Baringo County, Kenya: Implication for an Integrated One Health Surveillance
content: Leishmaniasis is an emerging zoonotic disease recognized by WHO as a priority ne-glected tropical diseases (NTDs) targeted for elimination by 2030. The disease is trans-mitted through bites of infected female phlebotomine sand flies and present in three main forms, cutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis. VL has two distinct epidemiological cycles: anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis (AVL) cycle, caused by L. donovani, and transmitted between humans and zoonotic visceral leishmaniasis (ZVL) cycle, caused by L. infantum with domestic dogs as the main reservoirs. ZVL represents the most severe clinical form and pose a public health risk due to high fatality rate. In Kenya, the epidemiology and transmission dynamics of L. infantum among canine population in endemic areas such as Baringo is poorly characterized. A cross-sectional epidemiological study was conducted in Baringo County, Kenya, one of the endemic foci for human visceral leishmaniasis. Blood samples were collected from 140 dogs Rabai, Sabor, Mbechot, Kapkuikui and Chemolingot and analyzed using Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Data on potential epidemiological risk factors and clinical status for dogs was captured using a questionnaire. Statistical analysis was done using Pearson’s chi-square (χ²) or Fisher’s exact tests to determine associations between seropositivity and potential risk factors. Bayesian Latent Class Model used to assess the diagnostic performance and accuracy of the two serological tests in absence of a gold standard. Overall prevalence of infection in dogs was 7.79% and 12.14% at 95% CI by the RDT and ELISA respectively. Multivariate analysis identified breed and clinical signs as significant risk factors associated with Leishmania infections. Local breed of dogs was more likely to be infected as compared to mixed breeds (OR = 11.92; 95% CI: 1.79–79.37; p = 0.010). Dogs without clinical signs exhibited significantly lower odds of ELISA positivity (OR = 0.06; 95% CI: 0.01–0.29; p < 0.001). Dogs with proper care and housing conditions had reduced risk of infection compared to poorly managed. Significant association with seropositivity was observed for sex, age, origin, and reason for keeping dogs. Diagnostic evaluation showed that RDT had a specificity and Positive Predictor Value of 100% with good overall agreement with ELISA, although sensitivity was 64.7%. Hence, RDT can be a reliable alternative screening tool compared with ELISA as reference standard. The study demonstrated the presence of Leishmania infection among the dog’s population in Baringo county, Kenya which is significant public health risk. Early detection and diagnosis of the infections in dogs through an integrated One Health approach in routine surveillance is essential. This will facilitate treatment and or culling of infected dogs and vector control subsequently reducing the risk of human transmission. Hence will go a long way to achievement of WHO’s roadmap of eliminating leishmaniasis by 2030.
